title: Windward Omnichannel — Concurrency Tradeoffs Labbook
content:
Purpose:
This labbook summarizes a 2-week POC for Windward (omnichannel retail chat + email summarization) focused on concurrency-driven tradeoffs between latency SLOs and unit cost. Goal: identify a practical serving configuration and routing policy that keeps 95th percentile latency under 350 ms for interactive chat while minimizing per-message token cost at steady-state and during microbursts.

Scope and constraints:
- Workload: mixed-user interactive chat (1–4 turns) + asynchronous email summarization (batch size 1–5 messages). Estimated production mix: 70% chat, 30% summarization.
- Traffic profiles tested: steady (50 qps), ramp (0 -> 200 qps over 10m), microburst (peaks to 1200 rps for 30s every 10m), and decline/backoff windows.
- Models: three model variants chosen from Redwood catalog for functional equivalence (same prompt template):
  * model-A-medium (fp16) — baseline higher quality, medium size, 6B-ish
  * model-B-quant (llm-q4) — 8-bit quantized variant for cost-efficient runs
  * model-C-compact — smaller 2B distilled model for fallback
- Hardware: Dedicated H100 pool (x4 nodes), Dedicated A100 pool (x6 nodes), Dedicated mixed burst nodes (g4dn-like for compact model).
- Serving features exercised: smart routing policies (latency-first, cost-first, hybrid thresholding), KV prefix caching warmups, continuous batching with max-batch-size tuning, per-request priority labels.

Testbed and instrumentation:
- Load generation: custom harness (windward-loadgen) that replays synthetic sessions derived from production sampling with preserved token-length distribution.
- Trace and metrics: Redwood Console traces + custom Prometheus exporters for qps/tokens, per-model GPU utilization, batch sizes, and queue wait times.
- Cost model: per-token GPU minutes amortized (hosted rates normalized to internal reserved costs), included warmup/cold-start tax and kernel scheduling overhead.
- Failure injection: node loss (1 node out of pool), forced cold KV cache, and induced GC events simulated by pausing a fraction of worker threads.

Key experiments (numbered for reference):
1) Baseline throughput/latency sweep (steady qps): evaluate p50/p95/p99 and batch size distribution across models under 50–250 qps.
2) Microburst resilience: measure tail under 30s bursts to 1200 rps; test hybrid routing that falls back to model-C when queue depth > threshold.
3) Cost-first routing: route 80% of requests to model-B-quant unless predicted quality delta > threshold (evaluated via lightweight heuristic on prompt length + signal).
4) Cache warmup policy: measure savings when reusing KV cache between similar chats vs cold creation.
5) Cold-start and node-loss recovery: time to SLO regain and SLA-violation percentage during outages.

Representative results (aggregated):
- Baseline sweep (steady 100 qps):
  * model-A-medium on H100: p50 78 ms, p95 210 ms, p99 360 ms, throughput 100 qps, average batch size 18, GPU util 65%, estimated token cost $0.95 / 1k tokens.
  * model-B-quant on H100: p50 85 ms, p95 240 ms, p99 420 ms, throughput 100 qps, avg batch 22, GPU util 58%, cost $0.42 / 1k tokens.
  * model-C-compact on g4-like nodes: p50 110 ms, p95 420 ms, p99 980 ms, throughput 100 qps, avg batch 6, GPU util 42%, cost $0.10 / 1k tokens.

- Microburst test (1200 rps for 30s, starting from steady 75 qps):
  * Latency-first routing (prioritize model-A until queue > 300): peak p99 observed 1.9s, 37% requests breached 350 ms p95 SLO during burst peaks, fallback triggered but had 8s queue flush for fallback conversion.
  * Cost-first routing (edge route to model-B): peak p99 2.6s, but only 18% breached SLO due to wider batching; however observed quality regressions in 6% of summarization samples (heuristic-detected).
  * Hybrid threshold routing (switch to model-C when estimated completion time > 400ms): peak p99 900 ms, only 5.2% breached SLO — best resilience but higher perceived quality drop for ~12% of chat responses (shortened summaries, hallucination risk).

- Cache warmup experiments (chat sessions with repeated context):
  * Warm cache reuse reduced per-token latency by ~22% and reduced average batch times by 14% for model-A. Effective cost saving ~8% on net token cost at steady state. Cold-starts produced ~40–60 ms extra per initial token generation.

- Cold-start / node loss:
  * Simulated loss of 1/4 H100 nodes: immediate drop in throughput; temporary queue growth led to p99 > 3.5s for ~2m before autoscaler rebalanced tasks to other nodes. Recovery time improved when had pre-warmed cache replicas and aggressive queue shedding.

Detailed numeric snapshot (selected):
| Scenario                | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | breach% (>350ms) | token_cost $/1k | notes |
| steady-100-A           | 78       | 210      | 360      | 12.0             | 0.95            | baseline
| steady-100-B           | 85       | 240      | 420      | 18.2             | 0.42            | quant benefits
| microburst-latency-only | 150      | 480      | 1900     | 37.1             | 1.10            | fallback lag
| microburst-hybrid      | 92       | 320      | 900      | 5.2              | 0.56            | recommended trade
| cache-warm             | 62       | 165      | 310      | 10.1             | 0.88            | warmup gains

Observations and interpretation:
- Quantized model (model-B) offers ~2x unit cost reduction but increases p95/p99 under microbursts due to larger batch windows created by continuous batching and slightly slower per-token kernels because of quantized kernel path jitter. It is a strong candidate for steady-state cost reduction but needs safety rails during bursts.
- Small fallback model (model-C) provides excellent immediate capacity to reduce SLO breaches if routing to it is fast, but the smaller model exhibits non-negligible quality regression for complex prompts — must be limited to short-turn interactions or used with strict quality monitors and function-call fallbacks.
- Hybrid routing (predictive thresholding) gave the best composite outcome: kept p95 under target with modest cost increase and acceptable quality loss when constrained to a narrow set of fallback-eligible prompts (length < 120 tokens, interaction type = quick-answer).
- Cache warmup is low-hanging fruit for chat-heavy workloads: consistent 20% latency improvement on early tokens and network savings on repeated prompts.
- Recovery from node loss is dominated by queue shedding and autoscaler policy; pre-warmed standby nodes and proactive shedding (reject or route to alternate region/model early) drastically shorten violation windows.

Recommendations (POC conclusion):
1) Adopt hybrid routing policy as default for Windward: latency-first up to 320 ms estimated completion, then predictive switch to model-C for known low-risk prompts, otherwise route to model-B when cost optimization is primary.
2) Implement conservative fallback eligibility: only for prompts with token_length < 130 and prompt_type in {faq, short-summary, product-info}. Add a lightweight quality estimator run on the first token batch to gate fallback.
3) Enable KV cache warmup for chat sessions with 30–45s retention for cold vs warm tradeoffs; capture user-session affinity to increase warm-hit rates.
4) Autoscaler config: prefer faster scale-in/scale-out windows for burst windows < 60s; maintain 1 pre-warmed node per 250 qps and 2 per region for critical customers.
5) Observability: add a simple per-request "fallback_reason" tag and sample full-response diffs for 1% of fallback events to monitor quality regressions.
6) Pricing note: modeling shows hybrid routing yields ~20–35% net per-token cost reduction vs always-running model-A, while keeping p95 within SLO for 92% of steady states and improving burst resilience.

Open questions / next steps:
- Run a production shadow test for 48 hours with hybrid routing and conservative fallback eligibility to capture real-client prompt diversity.
- Evaluate advanced quant-kernel tuning on H100 to see if quantized p99 can be improved without losing cost parity.
- Explore region-aware routing vs cross-region burst draining to determine outage resilience and egress-cost tradeoffs.
- Build a small ML quality predictor (binary: fallback-safe) and evaluate latency of running it inline vs as a heuristic.

Appendix: short commands and run ids
- harness: windward-loadgen --profile microburst --seed 20291103 --run-id WND-20291103-01
- console dashboard: /dashboards/windward/poc/2029-11-03
- sample jira followups: JIRA-WIND-79 (fallback quality tracker), JIRA-WIND-80 (autoscaler tuning)

Notes to reviewers:
This document is intended as lab notes — numbers are experimental and reflect our dedicated pooled cluster configuration. For public-facing proposal, we will produce a short one-pager comparing three recommended configurations (conservative, balanced, aggressive cost-savings) with estimated pricing tiers and expected quality SLAs.
